Spin
spĭn
v. (to draw and twist fibre into thread; used by Christ of the labour the lilies do not perform)
Old English spinnan. Spinning was the constant domestic labour of the ancient household — the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31 lays her hands to the spindle — which is what makes Christ's illustration bite.

Biblical Definition

Christ names spinning only to set it aside. “And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin” (Mat 6:28), “And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Mat 6:29). Luke records the same: “Consider the lilies how they grow: they toil not, they spin not” (Luk 12:27). And the argument is stated: “if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?” (Mat 6:30).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to spin as to draw out and twist into threads, either by the hand or by machinery, and figuratively to draw out tediously.

expand to see more

SPIN, v.t. To draw out and twist into threads, either by the hand or by machinery; as, to spin wool, cotton or flax.

SPIN, v.t. To draw out tediously; to form by a slow process, or by degrees.

SPINDLE, n. The pin used in spinning wheels for twisting the thread.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:28 — "And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:"

Mat 6:29 — "And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these."

Mat 6:30 — "Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?"

Luk 12:27 — "Consider the lilies how they grow: they toil not, they spin not; and yet I say unto you, that Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these."

Modern Corruption

Christ's argument against anxiety is not that provision is unimportant but that the Father who clothes the grass will not fail His children.

expand to see more

The lilies argument is a lesser-to-greater proof and not a counsel of idleness. Christ does not tell men to stop spinning; He tells them to stop taking thought — the anxious, dividing care that the word carries. The reasoning runs: God clothes a wildflower with a glory Solomon could not match, and burns it in the oven tomorrow; you are worth more than grass and you are His child; therefore the anxiety is not humility but unbelief, and He names it — O ye of little faith. The same passage that forbids anxiety commands labour elsewhere in the plainest terms, and the two never collide because the object of anxiety is the future and the object of labour is today.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the cure for anxiety in Scripture is doctrine about God rather than technique. Christ argues; He does not soothe. He points to birds, to flowers, to the Father's knowledge of what we have need of, to the futility of adding a cubit by worry, and to the priority of the kingdom. Philippians 4 does the same — be careful for nothing, but by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. The peace comes after the argument and the prayer, and it comes from God rather than from a change of perspective.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek netho (G3514), to spin; merimnao (G3309), to be anxious, take thought; oligopistos (G3640), of little faith.

expand to see more

Greek netho (G3514) — to spin; Matthew 6:28, Luke 12:27 only.

Greek merimnao (G3309) — to be anxious, take thought; Matthew 6:28, 6:34, Philippians 4:6.

Greek oligopistos (G3640) — of little faith; Matthew 6:30, 8:26, 14:31.

Greek kopiao (G2872) — to toil, labour to weariness; Matthew 6:28, John 4:38.

Hebrew tavah (H2901) — to spin; Exodus 35:25, 35:26.

Usage

"“They toil not, neither do they spin” — the lilies of the field."

"“Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.”"

"“Shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?” — the argument named."
